I have been obsessing about [Nikola](http://getnikola.com/) lately. I wanted to add a “categories” widget to the navigation menu. It took me three tries but I finally figured out a pretty decent way to do it.

Nikola is just a pile of plugins, and its build process is derived from [doit](http://pydoit.org/). There are many ways to plug or hook into the building process. I pored over the docs, especially the section on [Extending Nikola](https://getnikola.com/extending.html).

One twist to my problem was that I wanted to put the count of posts per category in the menu. Seems like a nice touch, and the theme I am adapting has that feature. But the `NAVIGATION_LINKS` configuration variable only allows menus that have `(link,name)` tuples in them. No way to pass extra text to the template.

Then I thought I could do the whole thing in the page templates. There are lots of variables passed to the template. If the site itself were passed, I could have done that. Alas, not so.

My first real effort was to create a Task plugin that generated the category menu separately. The plan was to render a snippet of HTML that I could include in any page template. The snippet generation worked, but then the templating methods slapped `<html>` and `<body>` tags around the whole thing. Not what I wanted! I either had to filter off those extra tags, go a level deeper into the site object, or find another way.

Then I went back to the idea of a Config plugin, that put the category links in a submenu of `NAVIGATION_LINKS`. Instead of [(link,name)]{.title-ref} tuple, I added tuples of the form `(link,name,count)`. In templates that were not aware of this extra struture, I figured that the extra data would be ignored as the templating system walked the list of links. Nope, I got a `Too many values to unpack` error. So this plugin breaks all existing page templates.

What if I passed the count to the template in a failsafe way? Rather than as a tuple, I tried *appending* the post count to the category link in the query string. So rather than `('/category/cat_foo.html','foo',3)`, I passed `('/category/cat_foo.html?count=3','foo')`. Then templates could check for the existence of this count key in the query string, strip it off, and use it to format the category menu. Templates that didn't know to check for this would still work, having meaningless query strings attached to the category URLS.

It worked! Except I started struggling with the next step of putting the category menu where I wanted it. My plugin was *appending* to `site.NAVIGATION_LINKS`. That list (actually a tuple itself) is rendered into the navbar in order, meaning the category menu would go at the end. I didn't want it to appear last in the navbar. So I started rewriting the template to walk the list of navigation links and select the category menu to put it first. Then to render the other links, I would need to rewalk the list, skipping the category menu.

At this point I realized that I was yet again trying to put a square peg in a round hole. I didn't want to add the category menu to `site.NAVIGATION_LINKS`—the data I wanted to add didn't fit there, and once it was there I didn't want it treated like the rest of the navigation links. I needed to pass the category menu as a separate bit of data to the template.

Finally, after reading through the source code and `conf.py` one more time, I found was I was looking for. The `site.GLOBAL_CONTEXT` dictionary can hold whatever you want, and *it gets passed to all templates*. So really I just needed to pass whatever data I wanted to `site.GLOBAL_CONTEXT['CATEGORY_MENU']`. I gave it a list of 3-tuples `(link,count,name)`. Then I adapted the page templates to put this category menu exactly where I wanted in the navbar.

This is an example where the answer is obvious once you think about the problem for several days. If I were a real programmer I probably would have gotten it done a lot quicker. But I did do something that a real programmer would: I committed my plugin to a [github repo](https://github.com/leingang/plugins/tree/category_menu/v7/category_menu). It needs some love before I am ready to submit a pull request, but it gets the job done for now.
